baseline: std::sync::Mutex on Linux (futex-based since 1.62; pthread-based in the 2020 run)
caveats: The favorable numbers (light and no contention) come from one 64-core machine running 32 threads, so every thread had a core.
lock-bench's critical section is one increment; longer critical sections make spinning worse.
The GitHub repository (zesterer/spin-rs) is archived and development moved to Codeberg; the star count is from GitHub.
The spin crate itself makes no speed claim over std; the belief tested here is the common one matklad's post set out to check.

Extreme contention elsewhere: 161.125953ms vs 113.030539ms (INTEL 120 cores); 63.898884ms vs 30.795793ms. With 32 threads on 4 core/8 hyperthreads (pthread-era std), heavy contention: spin avg 55ms, max 161ms vs std avg 21ms, max 23ms.

how_it_is_fast: Acquiring the lock is a compare-and-swap loop on one atomic flag with no syscall, so an uncontended or briefly held lock never touches the kernel. Waiting threads keep spinning on the CPU instead of sleeping. That avoids wake-up latency when every waiter has its own core, and wastes CPU when the lock holder has been preempted.
name: spin (spin::Mutex)
one_liner: Spin-based Mutex, RwLock and Once for no_std; with std available it trails std's futex Mutex under contention and ties or wins only when idle.
platforms: Any target with atomics; no_std
skip_it_when: Any program that can use std: std::sync::Mutex already spins briefly before sleeping
More runnable threads than cores: a preempted holder leaves every waiter spinning
Heavily contended locks, where it was 1.2x to 2.6x slower in every run
tier_reason: Independent of the crate's authors: matklad's published lock-bench, a rust-lang libs rerun, and third-party reruns, all with the benchmark code public.
toolchain: cargo run --release (2020 run); not stated for later runs
tradeoffs: Burns CPU while waiting and has no fairness by default (ticket locks are available as an option).
Priority inversion risk on preemptive systems: a low-priority holder can be starved by spinning waiters.
use_it_when: no_std code (kernels, firmware) with no OS to sleep on
Threads pinned one per core with very short critical sections and light contention
Interrupt-free contexts where blocking is not allowed
verdict_reason: The idea that a spinlock beats a sleeping mutex for short critical sections holds only with light contention and spare cores: there spin::Mutex was 1.3x to 1.55x faster than the futex std Mutex. Under heavy or extreme contention it was 1.2x to 2.1x slower in three runs, and with more threads than cores it was 2.6x slower with a worst case seven times the mutex's. The crate's own README sends std users back to std::sync.
workload: matklad/lock-bench: 32 threads incrementing counters behind cache-padded locks, 10,000 operations per thread, 100 rounds; 2, 64, 1,000 or 1,000,000 locks for extreme, heavy, light and no contention. Runs from January 2020, March 2022, November 2023 and May 2025.

baseline: An LRU cache behind std::sync::Mutex (hashlink LruCache), plus QuickCache and Moka
caveats: The independent run (September 2024) predates stretto 0.9.0 (May 2026); its author called stretto's mokabench results 'arguably broken', and no one has rerun 0.9 independently

Earlier independent mokabench run, S3 trace at 100000 entries: 0.121% hit ratio and 8.509 s vs 2.327% and 2.422 s for Mutex<LRU>.

evidence.quote: Stretto trails by up to 57 points
It performs poorly mokabench results (arguably broken).

hardware: Intel i9-12900H (2024 run); not stated for the README
how_it_is_fast: TinyLFU admission with 4-bit counters rejects new keys that are colder than the eviction victim, and sampled LFU picks victims. Inserts go through striped buffers that may drop items under contention, trading exactness for throughput.
name: stretto (Rust port of Ristretto)
one_liner: TinyLFU cache ported from Go's Ristretto; wins hit ratio only on small caches over skewed keys, and 0.8 measured broken.
platforms: Any Rust target with std; sync and async caches
skip_it_when: Scan-heavy or bursty traffic, or a cache sized to hold most of the data: QuickCache and Moka led there
You need inserts to be guaranteed visible: buffered inserts can be dropped
tier_reason: Current numbers are first-party hit ratios from the author's cachebench; the only independent data covers the older 0.8 line.
tradeoffs: Admission policy can refuse items an LRU would keep
Sync and async caches diverge by 5 to 20 points on some traces
use_it_when: Working set several times larger than the cache with strongly repeated hot keys (OLTP-like traces), per the README's own decision rule
verdict_reason: In a 2024 third-party run, stretto 0.8 reached a 0.121% hit ratio where a mutex-wrapped LRU got 2.327%, and ran 3.5x slower. Version 0.9's own README reports a fixed policy that leads only when the cache is small relative to a skewed working set and trails by up to 57 points otherwise. It gives no throughput comparison with an LRU.
workload: ARC trace replay: cachebench with 16 clients (README); mokabench with 1 to 6 clients (2024 run).

how_it_is_fast: ureq does blocking I/O on the calling thread, so there is no async runtime to start and no task scheduling per request. name: ureq (blocking HTTP client)

platforms: Any platform with std networking; rustls by default, native-tls optional
skip_it_when: You expect it to make requests faster; the measured difference from reqwest is zero within error.

hardware: AMD Threadripper 64C/128T (2022); Intel 120-core CPU (2023); not stated (2025)
how_it_is_fast: Each lock is one byte (Mutex) or one word (RwLock) with an inline fast path of a single atomic operation. Contended threads spin a few times, then park in a global hash table keyed by lock address, modeled on WebKit's WTF::ParkingLot. Before 0.13 the unlocking thread woke a waiter while still holding internal state, which lengthened the critical section under contention; 0.13 (2026-10-21) moved the wake until after release.
name: parking_lot (Mutex and RwLock)
one_liner: Compact adaptive Mutex and RwLock whose old '5x faster than std' claim predates std's futex locks; today std wins under heavy contention.
platforms: All std targets; wasm32-unknown-unknown needs nightly with atomics enabled
skip_it_when: Heavily contended locks on Linux: std's futex Mutex was 3.6x to 11x faster in three independent extreme-contention runs
You added it only for speed on Rust 1.62 or newer
tier_reason: Independent of the crate's author: a rust-lang libs measurement plus third-party reruns of the public lock-bench filed on the parking_lot tracker.
toolchain: Not stated; std side is the futex Mutex from Rust 1.62 onward
tradeoffs: 0.13 raised the MSRV to Rust 1.95 and changed the lock_api raw-lock traits.
Automatic eventual fairness and hardware lock elision were removed in 0.13.
Adds a dependency for locks std already provides.
use_it_when: You need features std lacks: upgradable or recursive read locks, downgrade, fair unlock, raw lock/unlock without a guard, no poisoning
Low-contention locking on Linux, where it was 13-27% faster than the futex std Mutex in the 2022 run
Targets where std still uses pthread locks (macOS), though no current comparison was found
verdict_reason: The '1.5x faster uncontended, up to 5x faster contended' claim dates from when std wrapped pthread mutexes. Against the futex-based std Mutex (Rust 1.62+), three lock-bench runs from 2022 to 2025 have parking_lot 3.6x to 11x slower under extreme contention, with only a 13-27% edge at light or no contention. The author removed the speed claim from the README in October 2026.
workload: matklad/lock-bench: 32 threads incrementing counters behind cache-padded mutexes, 10,000 operations per thread, 100 rounds; 2 locks for extreme contention, 1,000 for light, 1,000,000 for none. Runs from March 2022, November 2023 and May 2025.

how_it_is_fast: Each message gets an owned type and a MessageView<'a> type that reads fields straight from the wire buffer, so strings and bytes are not copied or allocated. A lazy mode defers parsing of nested fields until accessed. The owned path is a conventional generated decoder, which is why it lands close to prost.

platforms: Any; pure Rust
skip_it_when: You decode into owned structs and expect a big speedup; the owned path is within about 20% of prost either way.
You rely on tonic's prost integration and do not want to change code generation.

with an Intel Cascade Lake-SP 8275CL processor, running Arch Linux.

name: zune-jpeg (JPEG decoder)

baseline: std HashMap's RandomState (SipHash-1-3)
caveats: All numbers are first-party; the suite is foldhash's, but competitors' versions were pinned in rapidhash's bench crate (for example ahash 0.8.11, gxhash 3.4.1, fxhash 0.2.1).
The 'fxhash' column is the old fxhash 0.2.1 crate, not rustc-hash 2.x.
claimed_speedup: Geometric mean 4.67 vs 23.66 ns per operation for SipHash on AMD EPYC without native flags (about 5.1x, derived from page data) and 4.29 vs 22.17 on Apple M1 Max; against foldhash-f 4.67 vs 5.27 (about 1.13x, derived from page data); English-word keys hash-only 1.60 vs 4.26 ns for foldhash-f and 13.15 for SipHash.

evidence.quote: significant throughput improvement over wyhash and foldhash.
Wyhash and rapidhash, two of the fastest non-cryptographic hash functions available today, have their own seed-independent collision vulnerability in the C++ implementations.

hardware: AMD EPYC 9R14, Intel Xeon Platinum 8488C, AWS Graviton3, Apple M1 Max
how_it_is_fast: It uses the same folded 64x64->128-bit multiply as foldhash and wyhash, with foldhash's integer path, and processes strings in wide multiply-mix chunks from the rapidhash algorithm. No AES or SIMD is needed, so the same speed is available in portable builds.
name: rapidhash (wyhash successor)
one_liner: Portable rapidhash/wyhash-family hasher with randomized secrets; about 5x faster than SipHash-1-3 and slightly ahead of foldhash.
platforms: All Rust targets, portable (no AES or SIMD requirement), optimized for x86_64 and aarch64; no_std; const-evaluable
skip_it_when: Keys are attacker-controlled and the attacker can interact with the process: protection is described as minimal.
Keys are plain integers and you control them: FxHash still ranks ahead on Graviton3 (average rank 2.11 vs 2.27).
tier_reason: Public benchmark harness and run script (docs/run_benchmarks.sh), four named CPUs, release profile flags stated; numbers are first-party.
toolchain: opt-level 3, lto = "fat", codegen-units = 1, run with and without -C target-cpu=native
tradeoffs: DoS resistance: 'minimally DoS resistant'. The Rust crate randomizes secrets as well as the seed; the C++ rapidhash and wyhash with static secrets have seed-independent collisions (one led to a Node.js CVE).
In-memory hash output may change between minor versions.
use_it_when: General-purpose HashMap keys in libraries or binaries that must stay portable, especially string keys.
You also want a stable, versioned hash for persistence (the rapidhash_v3 functions), separate from the in-memory hasher.
verdict_reason: In its own suite, rapidhash's fast variant is about 5x faster than SipHash-1-3 by geometric mean on four CPUs, without needing target-cpu=native. Its lead over foldhash is real but modest overall (about 9% to 13% by geometric mean across the four CPUs) and large only on strings.
workload: foldhash's suite (hash-only, lookup miss and hit in a 1,000-element map, set build) over 16 key distributions, plus raw throughput charts.

platforms: Any platform Tokio supports

keep tail latency lower by a few orders of magnitude

hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X
how_it_is_fast: Every entry is allocated separately and published with atomic pointer swaps, so readers never take a lock or write shared memory. Memory is reclaimed with the seize crate, and resizing is incremental so no single operation pays for a full rehash.
name: papaya (lock-free read-optimized hash map)
one_liner: Lock-free concurrent hash table where reads never block; aimed at read-heavy workloads and predictable latency.
platforms: All targets with std
skip_it_when: Write-heavy workloads: the author says it falls short there and suggests alternatives.
Memory per entry matters: every entry is a separate allocation.
tier_reason: First-party conc-map-bench results published only as SVG charts and histogram images; no numbers in text.
tradeoffs: Allocator pressure and memory-reclamation overhead on writes.
Access requires pinning a guard; owned guards for async are more expensive.
use_it_when: Read-dominated shared maps such as caches and routing tables.
Async code that needs map access across .await points without lock-holding deadlocks.
Tail latency matters more than peak write throughput.
verdict_reason: The author reports papaya leading on read-heavy throughput and keeping insert tail latency far lower than dashmap, but publishes the results only as charts and says papaya falls short on update-heavy workloads. The claim holds, at most, for read-heavy use.
workload: conc-map-bench (bustle) read-heavy, exchange and rapid-grow mixes with ahash and mimalloc.

baseline: std HashMap's RandomState (SipHash-1-3)

The independent suite is run by the author of a competing hasher (rapidhash).
claimed_speedup: Claimed: fastest non-cryptographic hash of its class for all input sizes (charts only). Independent, AMD EPYC with target-cpu=native: geometric mean 5.01 vs 25.75 ns for SipHash (about 5.1x, derived from page data) but behind rapidhash-f at 4.68; average rank 4.31 vs 2.56 for rapidhash-f; tenkilobyte keys hash-only 119.67 vs 351.00 ns for rapidhash-f and 2103.16 for SipHash; u64 lookup hit 2.89 vs 2.03 ns for FxHash.

evidence.quote: Up to this date, GxHash is the fastest non-cryptographic hashing algorithm of its class, for all input sizes.
Gxhash requires aes and sse2 intrinsics. Make sure the processor supports it and build with RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native"
Hash has arbitrary seed-independent multicollisions, is not DoS resistant

hardware: AMD EPYC 9R14 (independent); project charts from GitHub Actions x86_64 and ARM runners
how_it_is_fast: gxhash processes input in 16-byte SIMD lanes with high instruction-level parallelism and mixes with hardware AES rounds. It reads past the end of short inputs with unsafe loads to avoid branching on length. On long inputs this gives much higher throughput than scalar multiply-based hashers.
install: cargo add gxhash (build with RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native")
name: gxhash (AES/SIMD hasher)
one_liner: AES- and SIMD-based hasher that is fastest on long keys but slower than foldhash or rapidhash on integers, and needs AES at build time.
platforms: x86_64 with AES-NI and SSE2, aarch64 with AES and NEON; no fallback, fails to build elsewhere or without target-cpu=native / target-feature=+aes,+sse2; no_std without the std feature
skip_it_when: Keys are integers, tuples or short strings: rapidhash, foldhash and FxHash were faster in the independent suite.
Keys are attacker-controlled: the 3.x releases have seed-independent multicollisions (issue #83).
You ship portable binaries or libraries: the crate does not compile without AES and SSE2 or NEON target features.
Safety-critical code: the README warns of aggressive unsafe tricks.
tier_reason: The project's own numbers exist only as SVG charts; the numbers used here come from the independent rapidhash suite, which has public code and stated hardware.
toolchain: lto = "fat", codegen-units = 1, -C target-cpu=native (required to compile gxhash)
tradeoffs: DoS resistance: seeded, but issue #83 shows inputs that collide for every seed in 3.x; a later report (#131) finds seed-dependent collisions above 128 bytes in 4.0.
Requires target-cpu=native or explicit target features, which ties binaries to a CPU family.
Uses unsafe out-of-bounds reads as an optimization.
use_it_when: Keys are long strings or byte buffers (hundreds of bytes or more) and you control the target CPU.
Deterministic hashes across platforms for a given major version are useful (the deterministic feature).
verdict_reason: gxhash beats SipHash-1-3 by about 5x in independent hash-table tests and is the fastest tested hasher on long inputs. Its claim to be the fastest for all input sizes does not hold: on integers and short keys, rapidhash, foldhash and FxHash are faster. The released 3.x line also has seed-independent collisions.
workload: foldhash suite as run by rapidhash: hash-only, lookups and set build over 16 key distributions, from u32 to 10 KB byte strings.

baseline: std HashMap's RandomState (SipHash-1-3)
caveats: First-party numbers were taken with foldhash 0.1.0 in August 2024; 0.2.0 changed string hashing.

evidence.quote: one with a 2023 Apple M2 CPU, one with a 2023 Intel Xeon Platinum 8481C server CPU, both with stable Rust 1.80.1.

hardware: Intel Xeon Platinum 8481C; Apple M2; AMD EPYC 9R14 (independent rerun)
how_it_is_fast: Each mixing step multiplies two 64-bit words into a 128-bit product and XORs the halves together, which mixes bits well in one multiply. Integers take a single folded multiply against random per-process secrets. The fast variant skips a final avalanche step because the benchmarks showed better bit quality did not make hash tables faster.
install: cargo add foldhash (or use hashbrown 0.15+, where it is the default hasher)
name: foldhash (folded-multiply hasher, hashbrown's default)
one_liner: Portable, seeded hasher built on a folded multiply; about 5x faster than SipHash-1-3 across hash-table workloads.
platforms: All Rust targets (portable, no special CPU instructions); no_std without the std feature
skip_it_when: Keys come from untrusted, interactive clients who can observe timing or iteration order: the README says it does not resist such attackers.
You need hashes that are stable across versions or platforms.
tier_reason: Public benchmark code (benches/bench.rs) with hardware, Rust 1.80.1 and flags stated, and the same suite rerun independently by the rapidhash project.
toolchain: Rust 1.80.1, lto = "thin", with and without -C target-cpu=native (foldhash suite); lto = "fat", codegen-units = 1 (rapidhash rerun)
tradeoffs: DoS resistance: 'minimally DoS-resistant'. Random secrets stop fixed collision sets, but the author states it does not resist interactive attackers who can learn the secrets.
Measurable statistical bias in foldhash::fast; use foldhash::quality for HyperLogLog or MinHash style algorithms.
Hash output is not stable across versions.
use_it_when: General-purpose HashMap and HashSet keys on any platform, without relying on AES or target-cpu flags.
Integer, tuple and small struct keys, where it is within a few tenths of a nanosecond of FxHash without FxHash's collision cliffs.
verdict_reason: Across 16 key distributions and four operations, foldhash-f is about 4.6x to 5x faster than SipHash-1-3 by geometric mean in its own suite, and a competing author's suite reproduces a similar gap on AMD EPYC. The win holds without target-cpu=native.

how_it_is_fast: glidesort scans for sorted runs like powersort but defers sorting unsorted stretches, merging logical runs and sorting them with a branchless stable quicksort only when needed. It interleaves several merges for memory- and instruction-level parallelism.

platforms: All Rust targets

Binary size or compile time matters.

baseline: String for short strings
caveats: Speed claims are unquantified in text; string-rosetta-rs results (run 2026-03-09) are SVG charts.

claimed_speedup: No numbers published in text. Stores up to 24 bytes inline in a value the same size as String.

evidence.quote: Stores up to 24 bytes on the stack
don't have to heap allocate so it's more performant.
*(`smartstring` is skipped due to how slow it is)*

how_it_is_fast: The last byte of the 24-byte value doubles as a discriminant and length, so up to 24 bytes of text fit inline with no heap pointer. Short-string creation and clone copy with two overlapping fixed-width loads and stores instead of calling memcpy, and accesses use branchless selection between inline and heap layouts.
name: compact_str (CompactString, 24-byte inline string)
one_liner: Mutable String replacement that stores strings up to 24 bytes inline in the same 24 bytes; avoids allocations for short strings.
platforms: All Rust targets (12-byte inline limit on 32-bit); no_std
skip_it_when: Strings are cloned far more than created: clone is O(n); an O(1)-clone type such as ecow or arcstr fits better.
Profiling has not shown string allocation as a cost: the rosetta-rs maintainers suggest String by default.
tier_reason: No benchmark numbers in text from the project; the referenced string-rosetta-rs results are chart images only.
tradeoffs: Uses unsafe code (tested with miri, proptest and fuzzing per string-rosetta-rs).
Heap strings grow by 1.5x rather than 2x, which can mean more reallocations for strings built by repeated pushes.
use_it_when: Parsing or deserializing many short strings that you may later mutate.
Option<CompactString> fields where the niche keeps the size at 24 bytes.
verdict_reason: The memory property is certain: strings up to 24 bytes are stored inline in a type the size of String, so they need no allocation. The README's claim that this makes it more performant has no published numbers, and the third-party comparison it points to shows results only as charts.
workload: string-rosetta-rs: creating, cloning, accessing and comparing strings of varying length (charts only).

hardware: 48-logical-core server with 128 GiB (Tweag); Intel Core i7-13800H, 14 cores / 20 threads (mimalloc-bench)
how_it_is_fast: Each thread allocates from its own heap of size-segregated pages, each page keeping its own free list, so the common path needs no locks or atomics. Frees from other threads go to a separate per-page list that the owner collects later. musl's allocator, by contrast, serializes threads on a shared lock, which is where most of its slowdown comes from.
name: mimalloc (global allocator)
one_liner: Rust global allocator for Microsoft's mimalloc: 25x faster than musl's malloc in a 48-core test, 4-54% faster than glibc on most real programs.
os: Linux (Tweag, distro not stated); Ubuntu 26.04 with glibc 2.43 (mimalloc-bench)
platforms: Linux (glibc and musl), macOS, Windows and BSDs; needs a C compiler at build time

tier_reason: A third-party mimalloc-bench run with public scripts and raw CSV, CPU, OS, glibc version and -march=native stated, backed by an independent wasmtime test.
toolchain: Rust targeting x86_64-unknown-linux-musl with mimalloc linked into libc.a (Tweag); C benchmarks and allocators built with -march=native (mimalloc-bench)
tradeoffs: Higher peak memory on some workloads: in rust-lang's rustc experiment (mimalloc 1.7 era) max-RSS rose 6-35%, and in mimalloc-bench lua used 80340 KB vs glibc's 66628 KB.
Adds a C build dependency.
Secure mode costs about 10% according to the crate README.

Allocation-heavy multithreaded programs on glibc
Short-lived processes that allocate many small objects

how_it_is_fast: rayon::join pushes one closure onto the current worker's deque and runs the other; idle workers steal pending halves, so work splits only when a core is free. A global pool is created once and reused, avoiding per-call thread spawns, and parallel iterators split ranges adaptively.
name: rayon (work-stealing data parallelism)
one_liner: Work-stealing parallel iterators and join; its published speedups are against sequential code, not against hand-split std::thread.
platforms: All std targets with threads
skip_it_when: Tiny inputs: the 1K-element quicksort ran at 0.41x of sequential speed without a cutoff
Uniform work that splits evenly into one chunk per core, where hand-split scoped threads have no scheduler overhead
tier_reason: First-party blog post from 2015 with the machine named loosely and no toolchain or flags.
tradeoffs: A global thread pool that other libraries may also use, which can oversubscribe cores when mixed with other pools.
Blocking inside Rayon tasks stalls workers.
use_it_when: Uneven per-item cost, where static chunking leaves threads idle
Many small parallel regions, where spawning threads each time costs more than reusing a pool
Recursive divide-and-conquer algorithms
verdict_reason: The authors' published numbers compare a 2015 Rayon quicksort with sequential code, not with hand-split std::thread work: 3.10x on 4 cores for large arrays, and 0.41x (slower) for 1K elements. No measurement of Rayon against manually chunked scoped threads was found, so its advantage over the default is load balancing and convenience rather than a measured speedup.
workload: Parallel quicksort using rayon::join on arrays from 1K to 1024K elements, with and without falling back to sequential sort below 5K elements.

how_it_is_fast: LeapMap is an open-addressing table where each bucket stores offsets to the next probe positions (leapfrog probing), so lookups jump directly along a key's probe chain. name: leapfrog (LeapMap concurrent hash map)
one_liner: Lock-free concurrent map using leapfrog probing; about 12x RwLock<HashMap> throughput at 16 threads on reads, with value-type restrictions.

baseline: std HashMap's RandomState (SipHash-1-3)
caveats: The independent per-operation numbers come from the old fxhash 0.2.1 crate, which uses the pre-2.0 algorithm; no independent per-operation numbers for rustc-hash 2.x were found.
The rustc-perf result compares rustc-hash 2.0 with 1.x inside rustc, not with SipHash.

evidence.quote: These attacks aren't a concern in the compiler so we prefer to use a quicker, non-cryptographic hash algorithm.
this means everything can collide for a hash table of size 2^n if all differences are in bits n or above.

hardware: AMD EPYC 9R14 (rapidhash suite); rust-lang perf server (rustc-perf)
how_it_is_fast: Hashing an integer is one multiply (plus, since 2.0, an add and a final rotate); there is no per-map state, no seed and almost no finalization, so the whole hasher inlines. 2.0 replaced the Firefox-derived design with a polynomial hash, a bit rotation that moves high-entropy bits into the low bits hash tables index by, and a wyhash-style routine for strings.
metric: time (ns per operation); instruction count for the rustc-perf run
name: rustc-hash (FxHasher, rewritten in 2.0)
one_liner: The rustc compiler's unkeyed FxHasher; fastest on integer keys, with no DoS resistance and known collision patterns.
platforms: All Rust targets; no_std without the std feature
skip_it_when: Any key can be chosen by an outside party: the hash is unkeyed and collisions can be precomputed.
Keys are long strings or byte slices; seeded hashers such as foldhash or rapidhash are faster there.
You are on pre-2.0 FxHash (rustc-hash 1.x or the fxhash crate) and your keys vary mainly in their high bits, such as multiples of large powers of two.
tier_reason: Independent numbers from the rapidhash suite (code and hardware public) for the fxhash 0.2.1 crate, plus rust-lang's own rustc-perf run for the 2.0 update.
toolchain: lto = "fat", codegen-units = 1, -C target-cpu=native (rapidhash suite)
tradeoffs: DoS resistance: none. The README states DoS attacks are not a concern for the compiler, which is why it uses a non-keyed hash.
Pathological slowdowns are possible on structured keys even without an attacker.
use_it_when: Keys are trusted integers, pointers or small integer tuples, as in compilers and other tools with no attacker-controlled input.
You want deterministic iteration order across runs (no random seed).
verdict_reason: On integer keys FxHash is the fastest hasher in independent tests, about 7x faster per lookup than SipHash-1-3. The published numbers are for the pre-2.0 algorithm, which collapses when keys differ only in high bits (7x slower than SipHash) and is slow on long inputs. The 2.0 rewrite targets those weaknesses, but its only published measurement is a -0.1% mean instruction-count change inside rustc.
workload: foldhash suite as run by rapidhash: hash-only, lookups and set build on 16 key distributions; rustc-perf compile-time benchmarks for the 2.0 switch.

the performance benefit of the cranelift backend varies between negligible and ~30% with the average speedup around 10-15% for a single crate compilation in

hardware: AMD EPYC 9R14 (rapidhash suite); Intel Xeon Platinum 8481C and Apple M2 (foldhash suite)
how_it_is_fast: On x86_64 with AES enabled and on aarch64, aHash mixes input with one or two hardware AES rounds, which scramble 128 bits in a few cycles. Without AES it falls back to a folded 64x64->128-bit multiply. Both paths are far shorter than SipHash's ARX rounds, and the output is not fixed across versions or platforms, so the algorithm can change to whatever is fastest.
metric: time (ns per operation, geometric mean across distributions)
name: aHash (AES-based keyed hasher)
one_liner: Keyed, randomly seeded hasher for HashMap that uses AES instructions where available; several times faster than SipHash-1-3.
platforms: All Rust targets; AES-NI path on x86_64 only when aes is enabled at compile time (target-cpu=native or +aes), AES on aarch64, folded-multiply fallback elsewhere; no_std with the compile-time-rng feature
skip_it_when: Keys are integers or small tuples: foldhash, rapidhash and FxHash are faster there in both independent suites.
You ship a generic x86_64 binary without target-cpu flags: aHash then runs its fallback path and loses most of its lead.
Hashes are persisted or sent over the network: output changes between versions and machines.
tier_reason: Two independent suites (foldhash's and rapidhash's) with public benchmark code, stated hardware and stated flags (Rust 1.80.1, LTO, with and without target-cpu=native).
toolchain: rapidhash suite: lto = "fat", codegen-units = 1, run with and without -C target-cpu=native; foldhash suite: Rust 1.80.1, lto = "thin", with and without -C target-cpu=native
tradeoffs: DoS resistance: keyed with per-map random seeds and claims DoS resistance, but a 2023 key-recovery attack that needs only collision observations (issue #163) forced a fix in 0.8.4 and yanked older versions, and an open 2026 report (issue #292) shows fixed input pairs on the AES path that collide for far more keys than an ideal keyed hash would allow.
Map size: ahash::HashMap<u32, u32> is 64 bytes against 48 for std's HashMap, because the hasher state is larger.
Needs a randomness source at runtime (getrandom) or the compile-time-rng feature on no_std; without either it seeds from memory addresses, which the project says should not be relied on.
use_it_when: Hash maps keyed by medium-length strings on builds that enable AES (target-cpu=native or +aes); it had the fastest URL-key lookups in the rapidhash suite, ahead of gxhash and rapidhash.

how_it_is_fast: Each worker owns a local run queue that idle workers steal from, and the number of workers searching for work at once is throttled so idle threads do not all contend. portable_simd tracking issue #86656 is still open; the API can change between nightlies.
std::simd chooses instructions at compile time; runtime feature detection needs a crate such as multiversion.
claimed_speedup: range-set-blaze from_slice (core::simd) vs from_iter: "On a representative benchmark, the speed up was 7×."

evidence.quote: On a representative benchmark, the speed up was 7×.
It is nightly only and enabled by the `from_slice` feature.
To enable SIMD optimizations, compile with the Rust compiler
This is a nightly-only experimental API.
Tracking Issue for RFC 2948: Portable SIMD
This crate used to contain several kernels with hand-written SIMD instructions, which were removed after discovering the auto-vectorized code was faster.

how_it_is_fast: Simd<T, N> lowers to the target's vector instructions through LLVM's portable vector IR, so one source compiles to SSE, AVX, NEON or wasm simd128. It lets you express what the auto-vectorizer will not do on its own: reductions over floats, lane shuffles, comparisons turned into masks, and early exits across a whole vector.
name: std::simd (portable SIMD, nightly only)
one_liner: Portable SIMD vector types in std; can beat auto-vectorized loops, but still nightly-only and with little published Rust benchmark data.
platforms: All targets (lowers to SSE/AVX, NEON, simd128 or scalar); nightly toolchain only
skip_it_when: You need stable Rust: use wide, pulp or std::arch intrinsics instead.
Your loop is simple element-wise arithmetic, which LLVM already vectorizes; arrow measured its explicit SIMD kernels slower there.
You ship generic x86_64 binaries: without target-cpu or multiversioning, std::simd is limited to SSE2.
tier_reason: The only numeric claim found is first-party, from one crate, with no hardware or benchmark detail next to it.
toolchain: Nightly rustc with #![feature(portable_simd)]; the crate recommends -C target-cpu=native
tradeoffs: Nightly toolchain required, with API churn.
Benefits beyond SSE2 on x86_64 require target-cpu flags or function multiversioning.
use_it_when: You already build with nightly and have a loop the auto-vectorizer cannot handle, such as a float reduction, a byte search or a run detection.
verdict_reason: std::simd can beat scalar code, but it is still nightly-only in October 2026, and the published Rust numbers are thin: the clearest is a single crate reporting a 7x faster constructor on clumpy integers, which also changes the algorithm and asks for target-cpu=native. Arrow found hand-written SIMD slower than the auto-vectorizer for plain element-wise arithmetic.
workload: Building a RangeSetBlaze from a slice of "clumpy" integers (long runs of consecutive values); the SIMD path detects runs of consecutive integers in vector registers.

baseline: slice::sort before Rust 1.81 (TimSort-style merge sort)
caveats: Numbers are from the authors' own suite, measured on a 2024 nightly before the merge.
rustc-perf showed compile-time instruction-count regressions on the PR, mostly from extra code generated per sort instantiation.
claimed_speedup: Random u64: about 2.4x throughput for N > 1e4 and <= 1e6; random_d20 and random_p5 patterns: about 13x and 17x at 1e6 elements (Zen 3). Binary size per u64 instantiation 2335 -> 5294 bytes (release).

evidence.quote: random shows a fairly flat ~2.4x throughput improvement for N > 1e4 and <= 1e6.
random_d20 and random_p5 peak at 1e6, with a respective improvement of ~13x and ~17x.
Both the stable and unstable sort implementations in the standard library have been updated to new algorithms, improving their runtime performance and compilation time.

hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X (Zen 3); Intel i7-5500U; Apple M1 Pro
how_it_is_fast: driftsort combines run detection from merge sort with a stable quicksort for unsorted regions, so already-sorted runs are kept and the rest is partitioned. Remembering earlier pivots lets it filter out values that repeat, which turns low-cardinality inputs into near-linear work. A small-sort tuned for superscalar CPUs replaces the old insertion-sort-heavy inner loop.
name: std slice::sort (driftsort, Rust 1.81)
one_liner: Since Rust 1.81, slice::sort is driftsort: about 2.4x faster on random u64 and far faster on inputs with many duplicates.
platforms: All targets
skip_it_when: Binary size matters more than speed (embedded, Wasm): each instantiation is larger; the authors point to tiny_sort for that case.
Large integer arrays where a radix sort applies.
tier_reason: Public benchmark code (sort-research-rs) with CPU, OS and rustc version stated for three machines; the authors also wrote the std change.
toolchain: rustc 1.77.0-nightly (6ae4cfbbb 2024-01-17)
tradeoffs: Binary size grows (2335 -> 5294 bytes per u64 instantiation in release).
Allocates a buffer of N elements up to 8 MB, then N/2, instead of the old N/2.
Panics when an Ord implementation violates strict weak ordering, instead of returning arbitrary order.
use_it_when: Default stable sorting on any type; there is little left to gain from third-party comparison sorts.
verdict_reason: On Zen 3, driftsort sorts random u64 inputs about 2.4x faster than the old stable sort for 10^4 to 10^6 elements, and low-cardinality inputs up to 13x to 17x faster. It is std's stable sort since 1.81, so third-party stable sorts benchmarked against older std overstate their lead.
workload: Stable sort of u64, i32, String, a 1 KiB struct and f128-like floats across patterns (random, low-cardinality, partially sorted, ascending, descending), lengths up to 1e7.

baseline: slice::sort_unstable before Rust 1.81 (pdqsort)
caveats: Authors' own measurements on a pre-merge nightly; detailed discussion covers Zen 3 only.
The authors note some ascending/descending gains do not reproduce on Apple M1 or older rustc.
claimed_speedup: Small-sort about 2-3x faster and partition about 1.2x for u64 on Zen 3; 1 KiB elements with 95% presorted input about 2.2x faster for N > 400 and < 2e4, rising to about 2.8x; binary size per u64 instantiation 4691 -> 3456 bytes.

evidence.quote: the new partition implementation contributes a ~1.2x overall improvement for `u64` on Zen 3. While the small-sort is ~2-3x times faster.
random_s95 see a large improvement for N > 400 and < 2e4, with a roughly flat ~2.2x improvement. For N > 2e4 the throughput keeps rising to ~2.8x.
For very small types `mem::size_of::<T>() <= mem::size_of::<16>()` a good counting or radix sort is almost certainly faster.

hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X (Zen 3); Intel i7-5500U; Apple M1 Pro
how_it_is_fast: ipnsort keeps pdqsort's introsort structure but uses a branchless Lomuto-style cyclic partition and sorting networks for small slices, which avoid branch mispredictions. It inlines only the tiny-input insertion sort and outlines the main loop, reducing instruction-cache misses.
name: std slice::sort_unstable (ipnsort, Rust 1.81)
one_liner: Since Rust 1.81, slice::sort_unstable is ipnsort: a faster, smaller pdqsort successor with a sorting-network small-sort.
platforms: All targets
skip_it_when: Sorting large arrays of small integers or floats, where a radix sort can be faster; the authors say so themselves.
Inputs of about 20 to 200 elements that are 95% presorted, which regressed.
tier_reason: Public benchmark code (sort-research-rs) with CPU, OS and rustc version stated; the authors also wrote the std change.
toolchain: rustc 1.77.0-nightly (6ae4cfbbb 2024-01-17)
tradeoffs: Panics when an Ord implementation violates strict weak ordering.
Small regressions for nearly sorted short inputs.
use_it_when: Default unstable sorting of any type.
verdict_reason: ipnsort is faster than the old pdqsort across nearly all measured patterns and lengths on Zen 3, mainly through a 2x to 3x faster small-sort, and it is also smaller in binary size. A few partially sorted patterns between about 20 and 200 elements regress.
workload: Unstable sort of u64, i32, String, a 1 KiB struct and f128-like floats across patterns and lengths up to 1e7.

baseline: str::chars().count() before Rust 1.60
caveats: CPU not stated; libtest bench harness
Small strings see no change (en_small 14 ns before, 15 ns after)
claimed_speedup: 4x to 5x faster per the author; en_large: 1,598 ns to 281 ns (3369 MB/s to 19160 MB/s); zh_huge: 82,622 ns to 15,053 ns; en_small unchanged (14 ns vs 15 ns)

evidence.quote: is somewhat consistently around 4x to 5x faster than the old implementation

how_it_is_fast: Counting chars in valid UTF-8 equals counting bytes that are not continuation bytes (10xxxxxx). The new code reads the string a usize at a time and counts non-continuation bytes with bit operations, summing several words before folding the per-byte counts, instead of decoding one char at a time.
name: std str::chars().count() word-at-a-time counting (Rust 1.60)
one_liner: Rust 1.60 made str::chars().count() about 4x to 5x faster on medium and large strings by counting a machine word at a time.
platforms: All targets (portable code, no SIMD intrinsics)
skip_it_when: You need grapheme clusters or display width, which char count does not give
tier_reason: A rust-lang/rust change measured with the in-tree libcore benchmarks; the CPU is not stated.
use_it_when: Counting chars in a &str on Rust 1.60 or later: call chars().count() directly
verdict_reason: The PR measured roughly 4x to 5x faster character counting on medium to huge text in English, Russian, Chinese and emoji, with small inputs unchanged, and it shipped in Rust 1.60.
workload: libcore char_count benchmarks: English, Russian, Chinese and emoji text at small, medium, large and huge sizes.

caveats: The fast path is for contains; the PR title scopes it to str.contains(&str)
Single machine and libtest's bench harness
core cannot use runtime CPU feature detection, so the path is limited to SSE2
claimed_speedup: 16-byte needle in a long haystack: 504 ns to 82 ns (5061 MB/s to 31109 MB/s); short needle in a long haystack: 677 ns to 73 ns; short in short: 27 ns to 12 ns; regression: bad_simd 84 ns to 97 ns

evidence.quote: x86_64 SSE2 fast-path for str.contains(&str) and short needles
benchmarks taken on a Zen2, compiled with

However, at the time of writing, it is only used

hardware: AMD Zen2 (model not stated)
how_it_is_fast: Two-Way must compute a critical factorization of the needle before searching, which dominates for short needles, and advances at most a needle length per step. The new path, based on Wojciech Muła's SIMD substring algorithm, compares the needle's first and last bytes against 16 haystack positions at a time with SSE2 and verifies only the candidates, so it skips preprocessing and advances by vector width.
name: std str::contains SSE2 fast path for short needles (Rust 1.67)
one_liner: Rust 1.67 made str::contains with short needles 6x to 9x faster in long-haystack benchmarks on x86_64 by replacing Two-Way with an SSE2 scan.
platforms: x86_64 only (SSE2); other targets keep Two-Way
skip_it_when: Repeated searches for one needle over many haystacks or non-UTF-8 bytes, where memchr::memmem is still several times faster
Long needles, which still use Two-Way
tier_reason: A rust-lang/rust change measured with the in-tree libcore benchmarks on a stated CPU family and codegen setting.
toolchain: -Ccodegen-units=1, nightly before 1.67
tradeoffs: One adversarial benchmark regressed (84 ns to 97 ns)
use_it_when: Already on by default for str::contains with short needles on x86_64; no code change needed
verdict_reason: The PR's benchmarks on Zen2 show contains with short needles in long haystacks going from 504 ns to 82 ns and from 677 ns to 73 ns, and it merged for Rust 1.67. One case got slower (bench_contains_bad_simd, 84 ns to 97 ns).
workload: libcore str benchmarks: str::contains with 2- to 32-byte needles over short and long haystacks, including adversarial inputs.

baseline: std::sync::mpsc before Rust 1.67: the original pre-1.0 implementation that upgraded between oneshot, stream and shared flavors at runtime
caveats: Numbers exist only in chart images (crossbeam-channel's plot, rustc 1.63.0 on a 2-core laptop).
No rust-lang measurement of the old vs new std channel was found; rustc-perf results on the PR were reported as neutral for the compiler, which uses channels lightly.
A reviewer on the PR raised the concern that spin-then-park behavior can raise CPU use compared with sleeping immediately.
claimed_speedup: No numbers in text: the release post says the new implementation 'improves the performance and maintainability', and the pull request points to crossbeam-channel's chart-only benchmarks as 'more performant in some basic benchmarks'.

evidence.quote: in this release the implementation is switched out to be based on crossbeam-channel
This release contains no API changes, but the new implementation fixes a number of bugs and improves the performance and maintainability of the implementation.
sync::mpsc is now implemented as a thin wrapper around sync::mpmc
the new implementation has also been shown to be more performant in some basic benchmarks
Machine: Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-5500U (2 physical cores, 4 logical cores)

hardware: Intel Core i7-5500U, 2 cores / 4 threads (crossbeam-channel chart)
how_it_is_fast: The channel picks its data structure when it is created (an array-based bounded queue, a linked list of blocks for unbounded, or a zero-capacity rendezvous) and keeps it, instead of upgrading flavors at runtime. Senders and receivers use lock-free operations on the queue and park only when they must wait, with brief backoff spinning first.
name: std::sync::mpsc (crossbeam-channel implementation, Rust 1.67)
one_liner: Since Rust 1.67 std::sync::mpsc wraps a copy of crossbeam-channel, closing most of the gap that made crossbeam the default recommendation.
platforms: All std targets
skip_it_when: You need several consumers or select over many channels on stable Rust: std::sync::mpmc is still unstable, so crossbeam-channel or another crate is still required
async code: use an async channel
tier_reason: No numbers in text: the release post and pull request state the improvement, and the benchmark they point to is a chart image.
toolchain: rustc 1.63.0 (crossbeam-channel chart, 2022-08-24)
tradeoffs: Brief spinning before parking trades some CPU for latency.
The public API is unchanged, so MPMC and select remain unavailable on stable.
use_it_when: Single-consumer message passing between threads; it is already the default
Projects that want to drop a crossbeam-channel dependency used only for mpsc
verdict_reason: Rust 1.67 replaced the channel internals with a copy of crossbeam-channel, and the release post says this improves performance. The only supporting numbers are in crossbeam-channel's benchmark chart, where it led the old std channel in every test, so the direction is clear but the size of the gain is not stated in text.
workload: crossbeam-channel benchmark suite: seq, spsc, mpsc, mpmc and select tests over bounded (capacity 0, 1, N) and unbounded channels, N = 5,000,000 messages, T = 4 threads.

baseline: std::sync::Mutex before Rust 1.62 on Linux: a heap-allocated pthread_mutex_t from glibc or musl
caveats: One run on one 64-core machine, with an increment as the critical section; real programs spend more time inside the lock.
The comment does not state build flags; lock-bench's own instructions use cargo run --release.
The same lock-bench extreme-contention case was rerun by third parties in 2023 (Intel 120-core) and 2025, with the futex std Mutex again ahead of parking_lot and spin (see those records).
claimed_speedup: lock-bench, 32 threads on a 64C/128T Threadripper, new futex Mutex vs the old glibc pthread Mutex: extreme contention 27.645506ms vs 58.506588ms, heavy 1.822707ms vs 8.10534ms, light 784.189µs vs 2.802436ms, no contention 1.189231ms vs 2.97886ms (2.1x, 4.4x, 3.6x and 2.5x faster, derived from page data). The old musl Mutex took 89.146548ms in the extreme case. Size: the pthread mutex 'is 40 bytes' and was boxed; the new Mutex 'only needs 5 bytes'.

evidence.quote: this new std::sync::Mutex avg 27.645506ms min 26.492286ms max 28.900528ms
this new std::sync::Mutex avg 1.822707ms min 1.674482ms max 2.081187ms
this new std::sync::Mutex avg 784.189µs min 663.889µs max 1.156756ms
this new std::sync::Mutex avg 1.189231ms min 807.39µs max 1.50386ms
The mutex implementation, for example, is 40 bytes and cannot be moved.
In 1.62.0 Mutex only needs 5 bytes for its internal state on Linux, though this may change in future versions.

hardware: AMD Threadripper, 64 cores / 128 threads (model not stated)
how_it_is_fast: The Mutex is one 32-bit atomic with three states: unlocked, locked, and locked with waiters. Locking and unlocking without contention is a single atomic operation; under contention a thread spins briefly, then sleeps in the kernel with FUTEX_WAIT, and unlock only makes the FUTEX_WAKE syscall when the state says someone is waiting. There is no heap allocation, so the lock is a plain value that can sit in a static or a cache-padded array.
name: std::sync::Mutex and RwLock (futex-based, Rust 1.62)
one_liner: Since Rust 1.62 std's Mutex, RwLock and Condvar on Linux are futex-based; the Mutex ran 2-4x faster than the pthread one it replaced in lock-bench.
os: Linux (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, plus a musl build of the old std for comparison)
platforms: Futex-based on Linux (1.62) and Windows (1.78), and today also on Android, FreeBSD, OpenBSD, DragonFly and wasm with atomics; macOS and other Unix targets still use pthread mutexes
skip_it_when: Code that needs lock features std does not offer (upgradable reads, fair unlock, raw locking); that is a features question, not a speed one
async code that holds a lock across an .await point; use an async-aware lock there
tier_reason: The rust-lang project measuring its own std change with a public benchmark on a stated machine; one run, and the build flags are not given in the comment.
toolchain: Nightly build of rust-lang/rust PR #95035 vs the std it replaced (March 2022); build flags not stated in the comment
tradeoffs: No fairness guarantee: a thread that just unlocked can re-acquire before a sleeping waiter wakes.
Poisoning on panic remains, which adds an unwrap or into_inner at each lock site.
On macOS and other non-futex Unix targets std still uses pthread locks, so these numbers do not carry over there.
use_it_when: Shared mutable state in any Rust program on Linux; it is already the default
Short critical sections under contention, where the old pthread lock was 2-4x slower in this benchmark
Locks in statics: Mutex::new and RwLock::new are const since Rust 1.63
verdict_reason: On the pull request that made the change, its author, Mara Bos of the Rust library team, ran matklad's lock-bench at four contention levels. The futex-based Mutex finished 2.1x to 4.4x faster than the glibc pthread version it replaced, and the lock state shrank from a boxed 40-byte pthread mutex to 5 bytes. This is the default every Rust program on Linux has had since 1.62.
workload: matklad/lock-bench: 32 threads each increment randomly chosen counters, each behind its own cache-padded Mutex, 10,000 times per round, 100 rounds. The number of locks sets the contention level: 2 (extreme), 64 (heavy), 1,000 (light), 1,000,000 (none). Critical section is a single integer increment.

baseline: Vec before Rust 1.45, whose push growth went 0, 1, 2, 4, 8
caveats: Numbers are aggregate figures from the compiler's own workloads; no microbenchmark of Vec itself was published.
reserve_exact and with_capacity are unaffected and can still give capacity 1 or 2.
claimed_speedup: Allocations done by rustc reduced by 10% or more; many rustc-perf benchmarks up to 4% faster.

evidence.quote: This change reduces the number of allocations done by rustc itself by 10% or more.
the capacity growth sequence is 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, etc.
sped up many benchmarks by up to 4%

hardware: rust-lang perf server
how_it_is_fast: The amortized growth path now jumps from 0 straight to a minimum non-zero capacity (8 for 1-byte elements, 4 for elements up to 1 KiB, 1 above that). Short Vecs built by push do one allocation instead of three, which matters in allocation-heavy code such as the compiler.
name: std Vec growth skips capacities 1 and 2 (Rust 1.45)
one_liner: Since Rust 1.45, a Vec grown by push starts at capacity 4 (8 for bytes) instead of 1, removing two reallocations for small Vecs.
platforms: All targets
skip_it_when: You need zero heap allocations for small collections: a single allocation remains, which inline-storage crates avoid.
tier_reason: The rust-lang project measuring a std change on its rustc-perf suite, reported in the PR and the author's follow-up post; no per-benchmark table in text.
toolchain: rustc nightly, May 2020
tradeoffs: Small Vecs may hold up to 3 unused slots; the PR author found no memory increase in practice.
use_it_when: Always: it is the default Vec behavior. Before reaching for SmallVec or ArrayVec, check whether reallocation or the one remaining allocation is the cost.
verdict_reason: Measured on the compiler itself, starting pushed Vecs at capacity 4 (8 for 1-byte elements) cut rustc's allocations by 10% or more and sped up many rustc-perf benchmarks by up to 4%. Part of what small-vector crates were used for, avoiding the first few reallocations, is now the default.
workload: The Rust compiler compiling the rustc-perf benchmark crates.
